A MESSAGE FROM THE THETA THETA
We have just learned that we are to have the privilege of enter
taining our brothers at the 1947 national convention of Psi Upsilon.
The purpose of this^ message is to give you some data concerning our
Chapter and our University, where the convention will take place.
FIRST,
we want to tell you how honored
the Theta Theta knows itself to be in
being accepted as the host Chapter for our
1947 Convention. We are
very grateful to
all the Chapters for their concurrence in
making a convention at Seattle an assured
fact. We deeply appreciate the good offices
of Brother Jeff Weed and the Brothers of
the Executive Council who endorsed our
invitation.
To show our
appreciation, we
plan as
hosts to make this Convention one that will
be long remembered.
Thirty-two years ago, in 1915, the Ep
silon at the University of Cahfomia enter
tained our
Fraternity. During most of that
intei-vening time we of the Theta Theta
have hoped that some
day we, too, could
ask our Brothers to be our
guests. We
wished for this because of our lack of con
tact with the other Chapters of our Frater
nity, and because we know that a National
Convention on the Pacific Coast would
bind our
Chapters together in spite of the
extreme distances separating us, and would
intensify the feeling of brotherhood that
cannot be better promoted than by actual
association. We look forward to this Con
vention week, knowing that our Theta
Theta brothers will gain an
appreciation of
Psi Upsilon strengthened a hundred fold
by actually knowing the Brothers from the
other Chapters, and by participating in the
discussions of like Chapter and Fraternity
problems.
We look forward to this Convention be
cause we are very proud of our Theta
Theta Chapter and its home at the Univer
sity of Washington in Seattle. We want
every Brother who can attend to do so;
we want to know you and you to know us,
and preliminary to our actual meeting in
June a few facts about Seattle, the Uni
versity and our Theta Theta Chapter will
serve to acquaint you with Psi Upsilon in
the State of Washington.
Seattle
The city of Seattle is the largest city on
the Pacific Coast north of San Francisco.
Current guessiag on its population sets a
figure somewhere between 600,000 and
700,000 people. It is a
metropolitan city in
every sense of the word and its modem
stores, hotels and commercial buildings
will surprise you if you have never visited
here before. Seattle is a
city of wide
streets; said to be the best lighted in
America. It is unique in that it is located
both on fresh and salt water. Seattle's har
bor is Puget Sound, our connection with
the Pacific Ocean. Directly east of the
business and manufacturing district lo
cated around the harbor, is Lake Washing
ton, a fresh water lake some twenty-five
miles long, which serves as the other
boundary of the city. Puget Sound and
Lake Washington are connected by a canal
and locks, which give passage to ocean
going ships through a smaller lake, Lake
Union, to Lake Washington. The Govern
ment Locks which ,
incidentally, are only
exceeded in size by those of the Panama
Canal, make possible an almost complete
circumnavigation of the city by water. To
the west across the waters of Puget Sound
he the peaks of the Olympic Mountains,
perpetually snow-capped and so close to
view that you feel you can reach out and
touch them. Running also north and south
and paralleluig the Olympics is another
perpetually snow-capped range, the Cas
cade Movmtains. Part of this range and
south of the city some ninety miles is
Mount Rainier, a volcanic cone 14,440
feet in altitude.
Seattle is a
city of hills and, as a result,
the views from the majority of homes are
breath-taking. No matter where you are in
Seattle or where you look, you will see a
sight of beauty which, because of its di
versity, is unmatched in any other part of
the United States.

University of Washington
The University of Washington was a
fact before Washington was a State. It was
established by tlje Territorial Legislature in
1861, the original site located in what is
now the heart of Seattle's business district.
By 1891 the University had outgrown this
original location and a new
campus was
selected bordering on Lakes Washington
and Union. This site comprises some 600
acres
sloping-gradually to the shores of the
two lakes and their connecting canal. From
every point on the campus one can see the
splendor of Mount Rainier, both the Cas
cade and Olympic Mountain ranges or the
clear blue waters of Lake Washington
dotted with sail boats, and perhaps a
glimpse of our
Washington crews
practis
ing for another fling at
Poughkeepsie.
Our first ten-acre campus has growTi and
so has our first frame building. Today the
great modem University of Washington is
housed in some 75 beautiful buildings,
modern Gothic in architectural style. Six
teen thousafid students are now enrolled.
The athletic plant consists of a stadium
seating 40,000; a modern pavilion, swim
ming pool, baseball diamonds and a ninehole golf course.
North, and located on
private property
adjoining the campus are the Chapter
Houses of the 34 fratemities and the 27
sororities of the University. The Psi U
house is one block from the campus.
Theta Theta of Psi Upsilon
The Theta Theta Chapter was estab
lished at the University of Washington on
June 10, 1916. Prior to this date, during
-December of 1909, a local society with the
name of Phi Kappa had been formed. The
thirteeip founders of this society, brought
togetjiex by mutual friendship as were
those of the Theta at Union College, from
the beginning set as their, goal a charter
of Psi Upsilon. The history of the endeavor
to reach this end is largely a
story of the
activity of the Puget Sound Alumni Associationj as our Alumni group was then
kno^fej P^i Upsilon had a
large and strong
body of'^alumni- in the Northwest. Every
alumiius gave strong and active support to
the local society. For several years peti
tions were presented to the annual Con
ventions of Psi Upsilon by members of
the society who were
usually accompanied
by one or more Psi U alumni from other
chapters. These Psi Us from other colleges
pressed for support of our
petition by
countless letters to their Chapters, the Ex
ecutive Council and every individual Psi
U that they knew. Their efforts and the
work of the Phi Kappa Society finally
achieved success, and the charter establish
ing the Theta Theta of Psi UpsUon was a
fact some thirty-one years preceding the
date of our
coming Convention. Sixteen
chapters of national fraternities were estab
lished at
Washington prior to Psi Upsilon.
Of these Delta Kappa Epsilon was estab
hshed in 1911. Alpha Delta Phi did not
follow imtil 1921.
From the first the Theta Theta enjoyed
complete success and placed itself at the
top of fratemities at Washington. Over the
years it enjoyed an enviable record only
to be broken by the necessity of closing
down during the late war, as did most of
the fraternities at Washington. With the
end of World War H steps were taken im
mediately in the fall of 1945 to reopen the
house and to
pledge an
entering class.
This, together with complete refinishing
and refurnishing of the house, prepared
the Chapter for a real rushing season last
fall during which a
large freshman delega
tion was
pledged. Now we believe we are
again headed for our
rightful place among
the fraternities of Washington.
Alumni of Theta Theta
The Theta Theta Chaptei; has been for
tunate in
having an
exceptionally loyal
group of alumni who, though having de
parted from the active ranks, have been
ever aware of the benefits bestowed upon
them by our
Fratemity, and have not for
gotten the reciprocal obligations each
Brother owes the Fraternity. As a conse
quence, our alumni, together with those
from other Chapters who are resident in
this vicinity, have given generously of
their time and assistance whenever called
upon.
At a recent regular monthly alumni
dinner held in Seattle at the College Club,

JOHN LACEY, BIRDMAN
The Editor of The Diamond was so in
terested in hearing John Lacey, Delta
Delta '25, tell abotd his unusual vocation,
that he asked Brother Lacey to write his
story for the readers of The Diamond. The
following is Brother Lacey s own story of
his work and his career.
I
CAN hardly remember when I didn't

When I was a small boy, my father was

a
great deal about them. The result was
that I grew up feeling sorry for people
who had no

glass.
My father owned all the bird books that

good pair of binoculars,
the large heavy Civil War variety, with a
large field of view." I wasn't a
strong boy
and Father encouraged me to go into the
woods and on the river.
My home town was Havana, Illinois. It
was located on the Havana River near
where the Spoon River flowed into it, the
Spoon River of Spoon River Anthology and
Edgar Lee Masters. I had a
shotgun when
I was nine and wore it out by the time

even went to the point of allowing hunters

These men were

willing to put up with me.
These swamp angels were market hunt
ers and market fishermen. They lived along

town at the time and admired their work.
I read copiously of Emest Thompson

When I was fifteen I went to Lake

was

Whfle I was

put
in the Long Trafl going from Wflliamstown

great deal about the
New England birds.
